1. # **INTRODUCTION** {#introduction}

   1. ### **Background** {#background}

   Software development units usually serve several process owners with a shared group of people. Their schedules hold only if the unit can see how workload, priorities, and staffing change, and can judge the effect of a change before it happens. This project addresses that need in the Software Development Unit in PuTI. This unit builds and maintains internal applications for non-academic process owners in Telkom University.

   The problem involves several stakeholders that have different interests. Process owners define features and sometimes change priorities late. The head of section and the assistant manager approve changes and assign people. The system analyst breaks down tasks, project prospect estimation, and approve/reject change requests. Front-end and back-end developers, the data manager, UI/UX designers, technical writers, and quality assurance (QA) staff carry the resulting workload. Process owners want fast response, the team wants a stable workload, and management wants launch targets met.

   An interview with PuTI supports this view. In the initial interview, the Unit reported issues such as project timeline are sometimes vague and workload is sometimes uneven because of personnel shortage. The unit also describe how it handles eight situations such as mid-sprint Change Requests (CRs), absence, new members, rotation, task overruns, blockers, priority changes, and bugs. Table 1.1 summarizesthese practices and the gaps they have.

##### *Table 1.1.  Decision practices reported by PuTI and the gaps* {#table-1.1.-decision-practices-reported-by-puti-and-the-gaps}

| Decision point | Practice reported by PuTI | Gap relevant to this project |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Mid-sprint CR** | The Head of Section or Assistant Manager approves after consulting the System Analyst. Handled informally in group chat or meetings. A task is dropped or the sprint is extended. Reported as fairly frequent. | Impact is discussed but not quantified or recorded. |
| **Absence** | Planned leave is known early and built into the plan. Sudden leave is covered by someone with the same role. No backup person per task. Delay is absorbed by extending the sprint. | No view of who can cover a task and at what cost to other work. |
| **New member** | Onboarding takes about one to two weeks. Capacity is raised gradually without a numeric rule. No mentor time is set aside. | Delay in velocity is expected but not estimated. |
| **Rotation or withdrawal** | The Head of Section and System Analyst decide by comparing workload across projects. Handover is a short briefing, not a formal process. | Effect on the donor project is judged by feel. |
| **Task overrun** | Noticed in group chat or by checking the project plan. No formal daily stand-up and no escalation threshold. Overruns are logged in the plan. | Late detection. Logs are not structured for learning. |
| **Blocker** | The developer switches to an independent task. Blocked tasks stay in the plan or board with a hold status. | No measure of capacity lost to dependencies. |
| **Priority change** | The process owner decides. Assistant Manager and System Analyst screen the request. Can add scope or reshuffle. Reported as fairly frequent. | Trade-off between added scope and launch date is not modelled. |
| **Critical bug** | Hotfix goes first and features work pauses. Bug-fix time is not logged separately during a sprint. | Effect on sprint commitment is absorbed, not measured. |
| **Capacity and tools** | Capacity is judged on three activity types (development projects, operations, tickets) with no numeric rule or buffer. Kanban board, spreadsheets, Git repository, and group chat run separately and are updated by hand. No automated time tracking. | No shared, current view of load per person. |

Three patterns stand out. First, CRs and priority changes occur fairly often even though features are locked during requirements analysis. The unit settles each one through discussion, and the consequences are often times unknown. Second, capacity is judged without a numeric rule, a capacity buffer, or a backup person per task. Third, tools run separately and are updated by hand. Together these make the effect of a decision hard to see before it is made, which makes the vague timelines and uneven workload the unit reported.  
The Scrum Guide (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020\) defines events and accountabilities but to each team how capacity is estimated and how changes are evaluated. Adding people to a project does not speed it up, because onboarding and coordination add effort (Brooks, 1995), and PuTI reports the same delay when new members join. Because the unit’s context (informal decision routes, cross-role members, and shared resources) differs from the standard, solutions can range from process rules to dashboards to simulation, each with different cost and risk.  
These problems need a way to assess the effect of decisions on workload and timelines before they are applied, using the unit's project data. This is the proposed solution of this project to improve decision making on workload, priority changes, and resource allocation in PuTI software development unit. 

2. ### **Root Cause Analysis** {#root-cause-analysis}

   The team analysed root causes with a fishbone diagram, using the interview findings in Table 1.1. Figure 1.1 groups causes into five categories. A Pareto analysis would need counts of CRs, overruns, and delays per sprint. 

   ![][image2]

   #### [*Figure 1.1. Fishbone diagram of the causes*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Lq2D-OHKn3kpHKGEjMaXk9qKPxg0WW1R/view?usp=sharing) {#figure-1.1.-fishbone-diagram-of-the-causes}

   CRs and priority changes pass through informal discussion. No threshold tells the team when an overrun must be escalated, and handover between members is informal. Capacity is not expressed as a number, no backup person exists per task, onboarding is informal, and some projects face a shortage of staff. Process owners add or change needs late, hotfixes and support tickets interrupt sprint work, and the same people serve several projects. Tools stand alone and are updated by hand, and there is no automated time tracking. Overruns are logged only in the project plan or internal notes, history is not structured for estimation, and no current view of progress exists.

   The root causes point to one core problem: decisions on CRs, priorities, absence, rotation, and new members are made informally, without a quantified and recorded estimate of their effect on timelines and workload. This lack of foresight, combined with manual and scattered data, explains the vague timelines and uneven workload that PuTI reported.

   

   

   3. ### **Problem Statement** {#problem-statement}

   The root cause analysis leads to these statements.

* Change requests and priority changes occur fairly often and are settled in group chat or meetings. This causes the impact of a change to be not visible before the decision is made. 

* No backup person is assigned per task, and members shared across projects do the higher-priority item first, by judgment. Capacity is also judged on three activity types (development projects, operations, and tickets). Which makes the workload cannot be balanced across members and projects. 

* Hotfixes pause feature work, support tickets wait until a feature reaches QA, and the time they take is not logged separately during a sprint. Overruns are noticed through group chat or by checking the plan, with no formal daily stand-up and no escalation threshold. Making delays and overruns noticed late.


  4. ### **Proposed Solution** {#proposed-solution}

  ### **I.4.1 Analysis of Alternative Solutions** {#i.4.1-analysis-of-alternative-solutions}

  The team considered three alternatives. All are viewed through the two BoK areas of this project, Data and Development. Each is described by its BoK perspective, application scheme, the business process the Unit would follow if it adopted the alternative, strengths, and weaknesses. To make them comparable, every alternative is shown on the same process: the mid-sprint change request (CR). Each lists the BPMN lanes and the flow of steps. Figure 1.2 shows the current process as the baseline.

  **Current process (baseline)**

  **![][image3]**

  #### [*Figure 1.2. Baseline BPMN Diagram*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/13oM2AReZ2VnQ5lOb91EQISmE8dzNMrtg/view?usp=sharing) {#figure-1.2.-baseline-bpmn-diagram}

* **Alternative 1: Integrated monitoring dashboard.** A dashboard that collects and displays current project information such as task progress, team workload, and delays. It helps managers see the current situation more clearly, but it does not predict what will happen if a change is made. Figure 1.3 are the business process if the alternative is implemented

  #### *![][image4]*   [*Figure 1.3. Alternative 1 BPMN Diagram*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/17JzYvugB0601drlffyOZGjMwsnGqAGiC/view?usp=sharing) {#figure-1.3.-alternative-1-bpmn-diagram}

  *Strengths:* addresses the missing shared view of work, since the Unit's tools run separately, are updated by hand, and have no automated time tracking (Interview). It uses data the Unit already keeps in its plan, board, and repository (Interview). As a data-driven decision support system, it centres on access to and analysis of data rather than on building models (Power, 2002).

  *Weaknesses:* describes the present state only. Testing a CR, absence, or rotation needs a model-driven system that can run scenarios (Power, 2002), so the impact estimate stays a manual judgment, as it is today (Interview). The dashboard is also only as current as the manual updates behind it (Interview).

* **Alternative 2: Rule-Based Workflow and Ticketing System.** A system that manages change requests, absences, and priority changes through tickets and predefined rules. It standardizes the decision-making process and records decisions, but the impact of each decision still needs to be estimated manually. Figure 1.4 are the business process if the alternative is implemented  
  ![][image5]

  #### [*Figure 1.4. Alternative 2 BPMN Diagram*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xCaf4w273d5XUTbONVDhxS6yPtmWRhr9/view?usp=sharing) {#figure-1.4.-alternative-2-bpmn-diagram}

  *Strengths:* standardises and records decisions that are now settled informally in group chat or meetings without a record (Interview). The decision log gives structured data on decisions, which the Unit does not have today (Interview).

  *Weaknesses:* the impact is still estimated by a person, as today when the System Analyst and Head of Section judge it in discussion (Interview), and estimates in agile teams stay uncertain (Cohn, 2005). Adoption depends on users finding the tool useful and easy to use (Davis, 1989), and the Unit would have to move work from its current tools into it (Interview).


* **Alternative 3: Digital twin with what-if simulation and decision support.** A simulation system that creates a virtual representation of the team's projects, tasks, members, capacity, and skills. Users can test different scenarios, such as adding or removing a member, and see how each option could affect workload and project timelines before making a decision. The system can also recommend the best action using machine learning. Figure 1.5 are the business process if the alternative is implemented  
  ![][image6]

  #### [*Figure 1.5. Alternative 3 BPMN Diagram*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/16MsoOWCWdbpa-mkwpMgSd_izfcR85NcU/view?usp=sharing) {#figure-1.5.-alternative-3-bpmn-diagram}

  *Strengths:* tests a decision before it is applied, which is the gap named in section I.2. Simulation suits the trial of new policies before implementation (Banks et al., 2010\) and is a model-driven decision support approach (Power, 2002). It can model onboarding delay by reports one to two weeks before a new member is productive (Interview), and Brooks (1995) explains why new members slow a project at first.

  *Weaknesses:* needs structured data on tasks, effort, and skills, but the Unit's data is scattered across separate tools (Interview) and has not yet been released to the team. Synthetic data limits validity, because model validity is judged by comparing output with the real system (Sargent, 2013). Simulation output is random and needs careful statistical analysis, so results can look more precise than they are (Law, 2015).


  ### **I.4.2 Selected Solution** {#i.4.2-selected-solution}

  The team selects **Alternative 3**, a digital twin of the Unit's project and team system that works as a what-if sandbox with decision support. The selection rests on three points.

* It targets the core problem. Only this alternative estimates the effect of a CR, absence, or rotation before the Unit commits to it.  
* It fits the eight situations the Unit described, each of which is a scenario to run and compare.  
* The twin ranks options and shows reasons, and the Head of Section and System Analyst still decide.

  The team rejects the other alternatives as the main solution for these reasons. **Alternative 1** shows what has happened but not what will happen under a change, so it would leave the core problem open. Monitoring is also the concern of the companion team whose data this project consumes. **Alternative 2** standardises and records decisions, but the impact is still estimated by hand and the Unit would have to adopt a new tool and enter data in it. The Unit can still adopt elements of it, such as a decision log or an impact checklist, independently. The project will use the decision rules the interviews support as simulation logic.

  **Prior exploration.** An earlier prototype of the twin used synthetic data because real data was unavailable. It was not checked against the Unit's own data, so this proposal treats it only as input to the design. Table 1.2 lists the planned features.

  ##### *Table 1.2. Planned features of the selected solution* {#table-1.2.-planned-features-of-the-selected-solution}

| Feature | Scope |
| ----- | :---: |
| F1. Scenario setup | Create a scenario from the interview cases, set its parameters, save and duplicate it. |
| F2. What-if simulation | Run the simulation, compute results, show the KPIs it produces. |
| F3. KPI and scenario comparison | Compare baseline KPIs with scenario KPIs, identify the best scenario. |
| F4. Decision support (machine learning) | Recommend actions such as a replacement resource or extra days, based on capacity and skill, give the reason for each recommendation. |
| F5. Reporting | Summarise scenario results and the recommended action. |


  Candidate KPIs are projected completion date and delay in days, load per member against capacity, tasks delayed through dependencies, whether the launch target still holds, and tasks dropped or deferred. The team will confirm the final KPI set with PuTI.

  5. ### **Development Objectives** {#development-objectives}

* Identify and document the decision points that affect PuTI's timelines and workload, and how each is decided today.

* Design and build the scenario setup, what-if simulation, and KPI comparison features so that a decision's effect can be assessed before it is applied.

* Design and build the machine learning decision support and reporting features so that options are ranked on capacity and skill with stated reasons.

* Validate the design with PuTI stakeholders for correctness, usability, and usefulness.

  6. ### **Development Benefits** {#development-benefits}

The unit head gets timelines the unit can commit to and a clearer view of workload against capacity. Project managers get a common process to plan against. Developers get a more balanced workload across projects. Internal clients get more reliable dates on the deployment of the system.

For the wider organization and the academic community. Other software units can reuse the problem analysis and the evaluation approach. The literature gains a documented case of choosing and testing a digital twin for a software delivery unit.

2. # **LITERATURE REVIEW** {#literature-review}

   1. ### **Body of Knowledge** {#body-of-knowledge}

This project refers to the Information Systems Body of Knowledge presented in Figure 2.1. The framework consists of several areas, including Foundations, Data, Technology, Development, Organizational Domain, and Integration.

*![][image7]*

#### *Figure 2.1. Information Systems Body of Knowledge* {#figure-2.1.-information-systems-body-of-knowledge}

Based on the scope and objectives of this project, two areas are particularly relevant: Data and Development. The Data area supports the processing, analysis, and presentation of project data for simulation and decision support, while the Development area supports the analysis, design, implementation, and testing of the proposed system.

1. ### **Data** {#data}

   The Data area focuses on the management, analysis, and presentation of data to produce useful information. Relevant competencies within this area include Data/Information Management, Data/Business Analytics, and Data/Information Visualization. These competencies support the transformation of data into information that can be used to understand conditions and support organizational decision-making.

   The Data area is relevant to this project because the proposed solution uses software project data as input for scenario analysis and decision support. Within the scope, data provided by the integrated system are used to configure scenarios, calculate simulation results, compare baseline and scenario KPIs, and generate information for decision-making. The resulting information is also presented through scenario results and reports to allow stakeholders to understand the impact of different project and resource conditions.

   

   2. ### **Development** {#development}

   The Development Area covers competencies related to the analysis, design, and development of information systems. Relevant competencies include Systems Analysis and Design and Application Development/Programming. These competencies support the process of translating organizational problems and stakeholder needs into requirements and a functional information system.

   The Development area is relevant because the identified problems must be translated into requirements and functions for the proposed solution. In this project, this area is applied during requirement analysis, system design, implementation, and testing. For the scope, the developed functions include scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI and scenario comparison, decision-support functions, and reporting. These functions are designed and implemented based on stakeholder needs and are evaluated to determine whether they support the intended project-planning and resource-allocation activities.

   2. ### **Theories, General Concepts, Models, and Standard Frameworks Related to Development** {#theories,-general-concepts,-models,-and-standard-frameworks-related-to-development}

This section describes the theories and concepts that provide the theoretical basis for the proposed solution. The selected concepts are related to the role of the solution within a Digital Twin environment, the simulation of alternative project conditions, and the use of simulation results to support decision-making.

1. ### **Digital Twin** {#digital-twin}

   A Digital Twin is a digital representation of a real entity or system that maintains a connection with its real counterpart through data. Jones et al. (2020) identify several elements associated with Digital Twins, including physical and virtual entities, their states and environments, physical and virtual processes, and the connection between the physical and virtual representations. Through these elements, a Digital Twin can provide a digital representation that supports the understanding and analysis of the represented system.

   In the overall PuTI project, the Digital Twin provides the environment in which actual software-development conditions can be represented and alternative conditions can be analyzed. The team specifically focuses on the sandbox or scenario component, rather than the construction of the actual-condition Digital Twin itself. The solution consumes project and resource information provided by the integrated system and uses it to create and simulate alternative scenarios.  Therefore, the Digital Twin concept provides the broader context for the what-if simulation and decision-support functions developed in this project.

   2. ### **What-If Analysis and Simulation Modeling** {#what-if-analysis-and-simulation-modeling}

   Simulation modeling involves creating a model of a real system and experimenting with that model to understand its behavior under different conditions. Simulation is useful when directly experimenting with the real system would be difficult, disruptive, costly, or impractical. Within software development, software process simulation can be used to examine project and process behavior and support software project management. Kellner et al. (1999) describe software process simulation as a means of addressing questions related to software process improvement, project management, and strategic management.

   In this project, simulation modeling provides the basis for what-if analysis. The solution allows stakeholders to create scenarios, configure scenario parameters, run simulations, calculate results, and compare scenario KPIs with a baseline condition.  For example, scenarios can represent changes in resource availability, task allocation, project priorities, or other project conditions. This allows stakeholders to evaluate the potential impact of a change before applying it to the actual project.

      3. ### **Decision Support System** {#decision-support-system}

   A Decision Support System (DSS) is an information system designed to support decision-making by combining data and analytical capabilities to help decision-makers evaluate problems and possible alternatives. DSS is particularly useful for semi-structured decisions in which information and analytical models can support human judgment without completely replacing the decision-maker.

   The DSS concept is relevant to this project because the purpose of the proposed solution is not only to run simulations but also to transform simulation results into information that stakeholders can use when considering project decisions. The tWinner scope includes baseline-versus-scenario KPI comparison, identification of scenario results, recommended actions, explanations for recommendations, and reporting.  The system therefore functions as decision support by presenting the possible consequences of different scenarios and providing information that can assist stakeholders in decisions related to resources, priorities, and project timelines.

      4. ### **Machine Learning for Decision Support** {#machine-learning-for-decision-support}

   Machine Learning (ML) refers to computational methods that learn patterns from data and use those patterns to perform tasks such as prediction, classification, or recommendation. In a decision-support context, machine learning can be used as an analytical component that generates predictions or recommendations from available data. However, the usefulness of an ML model depends on factors such as the availability, relevance, and quality of the data used for model development and evaluation.

   Machine Learning is relevant to the planned scope because the DSS component includes recommendations for actions such as identifying possible replacement resources based on factors including capacity and skill, as well as providing reasons for the recommendations. In this project, ML is therefore considered as a supporting component for generating recommendations rather than automatically making project-management decisions. Since the current scope indicates that synthetic data may initially be used, the feasibility and appropriate role of ML should be determined based on the available data and the results of further analysis.

   3. ### **Comparison of Development Methods** {#comparison-of-development-methods}

A Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) model provides a structured approach for organizing the activities involved in software development. Different SDLC models organize activities such as requirements analysis, design, implementation, testing, and evaluation in different ways. Therefore, the selection of an appropriate development model should consider the characteristics and needs of the system being developed (Sommerville, 2015).

For this project, three SDLC models are compared: Waterfall, Prototyping, and Iterative and Incremental Development. These models are compared based on their development flow, requirement handling, delivery approach, stakeholder involvement, testing, and ability to accommodate changes. The comparison is used to determine the development model that is most suitable for the development of the What-if Scenario and Decision Support System.

1. ### **Waterfall Model** {#waterfall-model}

The Waterfall Model organizes software development activities into sequential phases. According to Sommerville (2015), the Waterfall Model represents fundamental software development activities as separate process phases, including requirements analysis and definition, system and software design, implementation and unit testing, integration and system testing, and operation and maintenance. The model follows a plan-driven approach in which development activities are planned and scheduled in advance.

The Waterfall Model is suitable when system requirements can be identified and remain relatively stable throughout development. Its sequential structure provides clearly defined development stages. However, because the stages are separated, changes identified during later stages may require developers to revisit activities that have already been completed (Sommerville, 2015). This characteristic makes the model less suitable when requirements or system behavior need to be continuously refined during development.

2. ### **Prototyping Model** {#prototyping-model}

The Prototyping Model involves developing an initial version of a software system that can be used to demonstrate concepts, explore design alternatives, and obtain further information about the problem and possible solutions (Sommerville, 2015). The prototype allows users and developers to evaluate an early representation of the system and provide feedback that can be used to refine requirements and system design.

Prototyping is particularly useful when requirements are not completely understood at the beginning of development or when user feedback is needed to clarify the expected system behavior (Sommerville, 2015). However, the primary role of prototyping is to support requirement clarification and design exploration. Although prototyping can therefore support interface design and early requirement validation in this project, it does not fully represent the intended development process in which functional components are gradually implemented, integrated, tested, and improved until the complete system is produced.

3. ### **Iterative and Incremental Development** {#iterative-and-incremental-development}

   Iterative and Incremental Development develops a system through repeated development cycles while gradually adding functionality. Larman and Basili (2003) describe iterative and incremental development as an alternative to a single-pass sequential development approach. In an iterative and incremental process, the system evolves through multiple iterations, with each iteration providing an opportunity to refine previous work and add further functionality.

   The iterative aspect allows requirements, designs, and implementations to be reviewed and refined based on the results of previous iterations. At the same time, the incremental aspect allows the system to be divided into smaller functional components that are progressively integrated into the complete system. Each iteration can involve activities such as requirements analysis, design, implementation, testing, and integration and produce a working subset of the system. This enables feedback and findings from one iteration to be incorporated into subsequent iterations (Larman & Basili, 2003).

   

   4. ### **Comparison of SDLC Models** {#comparison-of-sdlc-models}

   The three SDLC models have different characteristics that influence their suitability for the proposed system. Table 2.1 compares the models based on characteristics relevant to the development of the What-if Scenario and Decision Support System.

##### *Table 2.1. Comparison of SDLC Models* {#table-2.1.-comparison-of-sdlc-models}

| Characteristic | Waterfall | Prototyping | Iterative and Incremental |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Development flow | Development progressives through sequential phases | Development focuses on creating and refining prototypes | Development occurs through repeated iterations and functional increments |
| Requirement handling | Requirements are primarily defined at the beginning | Requirements are clarified through prototype feedback | Initial requirements can be refined during subsequent iterations |
| Functional delivery | Working system is primarily produced after the main development phases | Early prototype represents expected system behavior | Working functionality is gradually added through increments |
| Stakeholder feedback | Mainly occurs at defined development stages | Frequent during prototype evaluation | Can be obtained after each iteration or increment |
| Handling changes | Changes in later stages may require revisiting completed phases | Changes are expected during prototype refinement | Changes can be incorporated into subsequent iterations |
| Testing approach | Testing mainly follows the implementation phase | Prototype is evaluated repeatedly to refine requirements and design | Testing can be performed within each iteration |
| System refinement | Limited once a phase has been completed | Focuses on refining the prototype based on feedback | Existing functionality can be refined while new functionality is added |
| Development output | Complete system after sequential development stages | Prototype followed by the development of the final system | Progressively evolving working system |
| Suitability for simulation and DSS development | Less flexible when simulation behavior or requirements need refinement | Useful for validating requirements and interfaces | Allows simulation and decision-support functions to be implemented, tested, and refined gradually |

5. ### **Selected Development Method** {#selected-development-method}

   Based on the comparison, Iterative and Incremental Development is selected as the development method for this project. The proposed system consists of several related functional components, including scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI and scenario comparison, decision-support functions, and reporting. These components can be developed gradually as functional increments while maintaining integration with previously developed components.

   The iterative characteristic is also suitable for the project because some system behaviors, particularly simulation and decision-support functions, may require refinement after implementation and testing. Results from an iteration can be used to improve requirements, system design, simulation behavior, and functionality in subsequent iterations. This enables the development team to evaluate individual functions progressively rather than waiting until all system components have been completed.

   The Waterfall Model is not selected because its sequential development structure provides less flexibility for a system in which simulation behavior and decision-support functions may need to be refined based on development results and stakeholder feedback. Although Waterfall provides clearly structured stages, returning to previously completed stages may become necessary when changes are identified during implementation and testing.

   The Prototyping Model is not selected as the main development method because its primary purpose is to clarify and refine requirements through prototypes. Prototyping may still be useful during interface design or early requirement validation. However, this project requires multiple functional components to be implemented, integrated, tested, and progressively improved. Iterative and Incremental Development therefore provides a more appropriate overall development structure for the proposed system.

3. # **SPECIFICATIONS AND DEVELOPMENT MECHANISM** {#specifications-and-development-mechanism}

   1. ### **Regulations and Disciplinary Standards in Information Systems** {#regulations-and-disciplinary-standards-in-information-systems}

      1. ### **Development Body Of Knowledge** {#development-body-of-knowledge}

   There are four regulations/standards that we will use in the Development Body of Knowledge. Each of the standards is applied selectively, and using the parts that fit the scope and duration of the project.

   **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (Requirements Engineering)**, this standard will cover how to write and manage good requirements. It is used for the solution requirements and the functional requirements of the system (scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI and scenario comparison, etc.). Each requirement is also traced back to a stakeholder need and forward to a test and evaluation. 

   **BPMN 2.0 (ISO/IEC 19510\) and UML 2.5.1 (ISO/IEC 19505\)**. These are standard notation for modeling business processes and software systems. In this project, BPMN is used to model the development workflow and the scenarios. UML is used in system design, for example use case, activity, and class diagram.

   **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 (Software Testing)**, this standard describes processes and documentation for software testing. In this project, only its test planning and test case documentation are applied. A test plan is prepared for the system, and test cases are written and executed for each functional increment, so that each iteration of the iterative and incremental method end with a tested piece of functionality

      2. ### **Data Body Of Knowledge** {#data-body-of-knowledge}

   There are two regulations/standards that we will use in the Data BoK, it is mainly from Indonesia Personal Data Protection Act, and ISO/IEC 25012 about Data Quality Model. Each of the standards/regulation is applied selectively, and using the parts that fit the scope and duration of the project.

   **Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection**, this law will set obligations when processing personal data. The data used in this project, such as member names, roles, skills, and leave records, is personal data. The project will use synthetic data first. If the real data from PuTI is given to us, member identities are pseudonymised, only needed fields are used, and access is limited to the team

   **ISO/IEC 25012 (Data Quality Model)**, This standard will cover data quality characteristics, for example the accuracy, completeness, consistency, etc. The implementation in this project is that the data used in this project such as imported activity data, task, capacity data is checked for these characteristics (missing data, inconsistent label, etc) before it is used in a scenario. And also aligning with the stakeholder on what good data mean in the project context.

   2. ### **Development Constraints** {#development-constraints}

      1. ### **Scope Boundaries** {#scope-boundaries}

   This project covers the What-if scenario and decision support part of the PuTI digital twin project. The functions in scope are:

- Scenario setup: Creating, configuring, saving, and duplicating scenarios based on the PuTI cases.  
- What-if simulation: Running the simulation and calculating the results and KPIs.  
- KPI and scenario comparison: Comparing baseline and scenario KPIs  
- DSS tools: Recommended actions, with the reasons for each recommendation.  
- Reporting: Summary of the scenario run and the recommended solutions.


  2. ### **Constraints** {#constraints}

  ##### *Table 3.1. Project Constraints* {#table-3.1.-project-constraints}

| Constraint | Sub-Aspect | Trade-off |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Economic | Development cost, infrastructure (local or free hosting), software licences, maintenance cost after project | Low cost by using open-source tools, but no paid simulation or analytics software, so features are limited |
| Production capability | Team competence (three members), development time (10 weeks), access to data from PuTI and Digital Twin Modelling team, use of synthetic data | All scope functions are finished on time, but the DSS recommendations are kept simple because the data is synthetic and the time is short, and results are not yet based on real PuTI data |
| Legal | Personal data protection, agreement with PuTI, open-source licences | Compliant with the law, but real data comes later (if any), so there is less detail about individual members |

Trade-offs have the largest effect on the design. Under legal, using synthetic data first protects member privacy, but it means the results show how the system behaves and are not forecasts for real PuTI projects.

3. ### **Development Mechanism** {#development-mechanism}

   1. ### **Development Systematics** {#development-systematics}

   *![][image8]*

   #### [*Figure 3.1. Development Systematics*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IzBqhMayU3wsBV6imUWqrh1bZHGDwMRJ/view?usp=sharing)  {#figure-3.1.-development-systematics}

   Figure 3.1 shows the development systematics of the capstone project. The system is developed using the Iterative and Incremental Development method selected in Section II.3. Iterative Incremental combines two strategies. Incremental development is a staging strategy: parts of the system are developed at different times and integrated as each part is completed. Iterative development is a rework strategy: time is deliberately set aside to revise and improve parts that have already been built (Cockburn, 2008). Using both strategies avoids a single-pass, sequential, document-driven process in which all requirements and designs are fixed before construction begins (Larman & Basili, 2003).

   Initial Planning and Analysis. Development begins with an initial planning and analysis stage. The team reviews the results of stakeholder interviews, identifies the required project and resource data, defines the initial functional requirements, and determines the high-level system architecture and the KPIs used for evaluation. This stage is deliberately kept lightweight, because detailed requirements and designs are elaborated within each increment. The stage produces two outputs. The first is an increment plan that divides the system into two increments: (1) scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI calculation, and scenario comparison, and (2) decision support and reporting. The second is a refinement list that records requirements, findings and required changes throughout development. The refinement list is adapted from the project control list used in iterative enhancement, which is revised after each iteration based on analysis of its results (Basili & Turner, 1975).

   Iteration cycle. Each iteration is a complete development cycle. It consists of six steps: requirement refinement, design, implementation, integration with the increments completed earlier, testing, and stakeholder review. Specification, development and validation are therefore interleaved rather than performed as separate sequential phases (Sommerville, 2016). At the end of each iteration, stakeholders evaluate the increment and their feedback is recorded in the refinement list. If the increment is not accepted, the iteration is repeated with revisions based on that feedback. If it is accepted, the refinement list is carried into the planning of the next iteration. Each increment therefore adds new functionality, and each iteration revises the functionality built before it.

   Iteration 1: Simulation and KPI. The first iteration refines the requirements for scenario configuration and evaluation. It designs the scenario parameters, the simulation inputs and outputs, the KPI calculations, and the comparison between scenarios. It then implements the scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI calculation, and baseline-versus-scenario comparison functions. The increment is deployed as the base prototype, tested, and reviewed by stakeholders. Findings from testing and stakeholder review are recorded in the refinement list. Development then proceeds directly to the second iteration, and the rework for Increment 1 is scheduled there.

   Iteration 2: DSS and Reporting. The second iteration refines its requirements, including the findings recorded for Increment 1\. It then designs and implements the decision-support and reporting functions. The system uses scenario results and KPI comparisons to generate recommendations for resource allocation and project planning. These recommendations are based on defined decision criteria: member capacity, skills, workload, and the potential effects of alternative scenarios. Each recommendation includes supporting reasons so that stakeholders can understand and evaluate it. The recommendations support stakeholder judgment rather than automatically determining project-management decisions. In the same iteration, Increment 1 is fixed and refined based on its recorded findings. Scheduling rework on previously built parts in a later iteration is a defining characteristic of iterative development (Cockburn, 2008). The new and revised functions are then integrated and tested, including regression testing to confirm that the existing functions still work correctly, and the result is reviewed by stakeholders. If the increment is not accepted, the iteration will be fixed before system testing.

   Final Evaluation and Release. All increments are integrated and evaluated during the iterations, so the final stage does not integrate components. Instead, it focuses on system testing of the complete system and on stakeholder acceptance evaluation. The results are used to make final refinements before the final version of the system is produced..

   #### 

      2. ### **Data Collection Mechanism** {#data-collection-mechanism}

   Data collection is conducted to support requirements analysis, scenario configuration, simulation, decision support, and system evaluation. The project uses both stakeholder information and software project data. Stakeholder information is obtained through interviews, while project and resource data are obtained from available records or systems provided by PuTI. If the required real data are not yet available during the initial development stage, synthetic data may be used to support early development and testing.

   The stakeholders involved in data collection are selected based on their roles in software project planning and decision-making. Interviews are used to understand current practices, decision scenarios, project constraints, and stakeholder expectations for the proposed solution. The existing interviews have covered situations including change requests, member absence, new members, rotation, task overruns, blockers, priority changes, and critical bugs.

   ##### *Table 3.2. Data Collection Mechanism* {#table-3.2.-data-collection-mechanism}

| Data Source | Data Required | Collection Mechanism | Purpose |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| PuTI stakeholders | Current decision-making process, project scenarios, system requirements, and expected outputs | Semi-structured interviews | Identify requirements and define relevant what-if scenarios |
| Project and task records | Task information, status, estimated or actual effort, project stages, and dependencies, where available | Existing system records and project documents | Provide input for scenario configuration and simulation |
| Resource information | Member role, skill, capacity or availability, and assignment information, where available | Existing records provided by PuTI | Support workload analysis, resource allocation scenarios, and decision support |
| Synthetic project data | Representative project, task, and resource data | Generated based on defined system requirements and scenario structures | Support initial implementation and testing when real data are unavailable |
| Stakeholder feedback | Feedback on system validity, usability, and usefulness | Evaluation instrument and stakeholder feedback session | Evaluate whether the developed solution supports stakeholder needs |

   Stakeholder interviews are conducted using a semi-structured interview protocol. The interview questions are organized around the project and resource decisions identified during the problem analysis, including change requests, member absence, new members, rotation or withdrawal, task overruns, blockers, priority changes, and critical bugs. A semi-structured format is used to maintain a consistent set of discussion topics while allowing follow-up questions when further clarification is required.

   Interview respondents are selected purposively based on their involvement in software project planning, resource allocation, and decision-making within PuTI. Relevant respondents include the Head of Section, Assistant Manager, System Analyst, and other personnel directly involved in the processes being analyzed. These respondents are selected because their roles involve activities such as approving project changes, assigning personnel, estimating work, and evaluating project conditions. The interview questions and transcripts are documented as data collection instruments in the project appendices.

   For system data, the project will use available project, task, and resource records from PuTI where access is provided. Required data may include task information, status, estimated or actual effort, project stages, dependencies, member roles, skills, capacity or availability, and assignments. The project currently does not assume that all required historical data will be available. Therefore, the final data fields, number of records, extraction mechanism, data format, and tools used will be specified after access to PuTI data has been confirmed. When operational data are unavailable, synthetic data representing the required project and resource structures may be used during early development and testing.

   If real personnel-related data are provided, the data-handling process will follow the privacy and data-quality requirements defined in Section III.1. Only data required for the project will be used, and personally identifiable information will be pseudonymized where appropriate. Before project data are used as simulation or decision-support inputs, they will also be checked for issues such as missing values, inconsistent labels, and incomplete records.

      3. ### **Validation and Evaluation Mechanism** {#validation-and-evaluation-mechanism}

   Validation and evaluation are conducted throughout the iterative development process and after the integration of the system. The purpose is to determine whether the developed functions operate according to their requirements, whether the simulation and decision-support results are reasonable for the defined scenarios, and whether stakeholders consider the resulting solution valid, usable, and useful for supporting their decisions.

   The first mechanism is functional validation. Functional testing is conducted for each increment to verify whether the implemented functions produce the expected behavior based on defined inputs and requirements. Test cases are prepared for the main functions, including scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI and scenario comparison, decision-support functions, and reporting. The expected and actual results are compared to determine whether each function satisfies its requirements.

   The second mechanism is simulation and decision-support result validation. Selected scenarios are evaluated by comparing their inputs, expected behavior, and generated results. For example, a scenario involving reduced resource availability should reflect the corresponding changes in workload, capacity, or project-related KPIs according to the rules implemented in the system. The purpose of this validation is not to claim that the system can perfectly predict future project conditions, but to verify that its outputs are consistent with the implemented model, assumptions, and defined scenario logic.

   Expected results for representative scenarios will be established through independently calculated examples and predefined test cases. Relevant stakeholders will also be consulted to assess whether the assumptions used in the simulation reasonably reflect the decision-making conditions being modeled. This allows the evaluation to distinguish between correct implementation of simulation rules and the appropriateness of the underlying assumptions.

   The third mechanism is stakeholder evaluation. Relevant PuTI stakeholders involved in software project planning, resource allocation, and decision-making  will be asked to evaluate the developed solution. Stakeholders may include roles such as the Head of Section, Assistant Manager, System Analyst, or other personnel involved in the processes represented by the system. These roles are relevant because the current process assigns the project-change and resource-allocation decisions to management and the System Analyst.

   Stakeholder feedback will be collected using a structured questionnaire and semi-structured feedback questions after stakeholders have reviewed or interacted with representative scenarios in the system. The questionnaire will evaluate three dimensions aligned with the development objectives and intended use of the system: correctness, usability, and usefulness. Correctness evaluates whether the scenarios, KPIs, and decision-support outputs appropriately represent the project conditions and expected system behavior. Usability evaluates whether the system and the information presented are understandable and easy to use. Usefulness evaluates whether the scenario comparison and decision-support information assists stakeholders in evaluating project and resource decisions.

   Closed-ended questionnaire items will use a Likert-type response scale, while open-ended questions will allow stakeholders to provide explanations, identify problems, and suggest improvements. The questionnaire results will be summarized descriptively for each evaluation dimension, while qualitative feedback will be reviewed to identify recurring issues and recommendations for system refinement. The final evaluation instrument and its supporting references will be documented before stakeholder evaluation

   ##### *Table 3.3. Validation and Evaluation Mechanism* {#table-3.3.-validation-and-evaluation-mechanism}

| Evaluation | Object | Mechanism | Evaluator | Expected Result |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Functional validation | System functions | Test cases comparing expected and actual outputs | Development team | Functions operate according to defined requirements |
| Simulation/result validation | Scenario and KPI outputs | Scenario-based checking of inputs, rules, and resulting outputs | Development team and relevant stakeholder | Results are consistent with defined assumptions and scenario logic |
| Decision-support validation | Recommendations or decision-support information | Review of recommendation/output relevance and supporting reasons | Relevant PuTI stakeholders | Decision-support output is understandable and reasonable |
| Stakeholder evaluation | Integrated system | Structured evaluation instrument and open-ended feedback | Relevant PuTI stakeholders | Evidence regarding validity, usability, usefulness, and areas for improvement |

4. # **OUTCOME OF SOLUTION DEVELOPMENT**

   1. ### **Iteration 1 (Simulation & KPI)**

      1. ### **Planning**

The planning stage of Iteration 1 identifies the functional scope, decision scenarios, and data requirements of the proposed What-if Scenario and Decision Support System. The analysis draws on the stakeholder interview findings documented in Chapter I and the development objectives defined in the proposal. It focuses on translating the identified decision-making problems into preliminary system requirements that guide subsequent design and development activities. As part of the integrated Digital Twin solution, the proposed system is intended to use baseline project and resource information provided through the companion team's components. Iteration 1 implements the scenario setup, what-if simulation, and KPI comparison requirements (FR-01 to FR-06 in Table 4.1), while the decision support and reporting requirements (FR-07 to FR-09) are carried into Iteration 2.

   **Stakeholder and Functional Requirements**

   The stakeholder interviews identified several recurring situations that influence workload, project schedules, and resource allocation. These include mid-sprint change requests, member absence, new member onboarding, member rotation or withdrawal, task overruns, blockers, priority changes, and critical bugs. The interviews also indicated that the consequences of these situations are generally assessed through discussions and managerial judgment rather than quantified scenario comparisons.

   Based on these findings, five principal functional areas were identified: scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI and scenario comparison, decision support, and reporting. Table 4.1 presents the preliminary functional requirements derived from these areas.

   ##### *Table 4.1. Preliminary Functional Requirements* {#table-4.1.-preliminary-functional-requirements}

| ID | Functional Area | Requirement |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| FR-01 | Scenario Setup | The system should allow users to create scenarios based on supported decision situations. |
| FR-02 | Scenario Setup | The system should allow users to configure scenario parameters and save and duplicate scenarios. |
| FR-03 | What-if Simulation | The system should calculate the effects of scenario changes using defined simulation rules. |
| FR-04 | What-if Simulation | The system should display simulation results, including affected project and resource conditions. |
| FR-05 | KPI Comparison | The system should calculate relevant KPIs based on simulated scenario results. |
| FR-06 | KPI Comparison | The system should compare baseline KPIs with KPIs calculated for alternative scenarios. |
| FR-07 | Decision Support | The system should provide recommendations based on defined decision criteria. |
| FR-08 | Decision Support | The system should provide explanations supporting the generated recommendations. |
| FR-09 | Reporting | The system should summarize scenario results, KPI comparisons, and recommended actions. |

   **Decision Scenario Analysis**

   The decision scenario analysis identifies the operational changes that the proposed system is intended to examine. Eight decision situations were identified through stakeholder interviews, as described in Table 1.1. These situations involve changes in project scope, resource availability, task progress, and priorities. Each situation provides a potential basis for configuring a what-if scenario. Table 4.2 summarizes the current practices, identified problems, and potential simulation parameters associated with these situations.

   ##### *Table 4.2. Preliminary Decision Scenario Analysis* {#table-4.2.-preliminary-decision-scenario-analysis}

| Decision Situation | Current Practice | Identified Problem | Potential Simulation Parameters |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Mid-sprint Change Request | Change requests are approved through discussions involving the Head of Section or Assistant Manager and the System Analyst. Tasks may be removed or the sprint extended. | The impact of changes is not quantified or systematically recorded. | Additional tasks, estimated effort, affected sprint, and target date. |
| Member Absence | Planned leave is considered during planning, while unexpected absence is handled by assigning another member with a similar role. | The impact of reduced availability and reassignment on other tasks is not clearly measured. | Unavailable member, absence duration, affected tasks, and remaining capacity. |
| New Member | New members undergo an onboarding period of approximately one to two weeks, with capacity increasing gradually. | The expected reduction in productivity during onboarding is not quantitatively estimated, and mentor time is not explicitly allocated. | Member role, skills, onboarding duration, and available capacity. |
| Member Rotation or Withdrawal | The Head of Section and System Analyst decide on member transfers by comparing workloads across projects. Handover is conducted through a short briefing. | The impact of resource transfers on the original project is assessed through judgment. | Transferred member, affected projects, existing assignments, and available capacity. |
| Task Overrun | Task overruns are identified through group discussions or reviews of project plans. | Overruns may be detected late, and their effects are not systematically evaluated. | Affected task, original estimated effort, revised effort, and remaining work. |
| Task Blocker | Developers switch to independent tasks while blocked tasks remain on hold. | The capacity lost due to task dependencies is not quantitatively measured. | Blocked task, dependency relationships, and estimated blocking duration. |
| Priority Change | Process owners determine priorities, while the Assistant Manager and System Analyst review the requested changes. | The trade-offs between changes in scope, workload, and project timelines are not modeled. | Revised task priority, affected tasks, estimated effort, and target date. |
| Critical Bug | Critical bugs are prioritized, temporarily interrupting planned feature development. | Bug-fixing time is not logged separately, making its impact on sprint commitments difficult to measure. | Bug-fixing effort, assigned resources, affected tasks, and available capacity. |

   The analysis indicates that the identified situations share a common need to evaluate the potential consequences of project and resource changes before decisions are implemented. Although the situations differ in their causes and operational conditions, they may affect related aspects of project performance, including resource capacity, task allocation, dependencies, and completion timelines.

   The potential simulation parameters presented in Table 4.2 provide an initial basis for defining scenario inputs during system design. These parameters are preliminary and do not represent finalized simulation rules. The selection and detailed configuration of scenarios will depend on data availability, system integration requirements, and further stakeholder clarification*.*

      2. ### **Design**

   The system design translates the functional requirements in Table 4.1, the decision scenarios in Table 4.2, and the data requirements in Tables 4.3 and 4.4 into a design that can be implemented in the iterative increments defined in Section III.3.1. The design is documented with BPMN 2.0 for the business process and UML 2.5.1 for the system structure and behaviour. The design covers the system architecture, use cases, the to-be process, the data model, the simulation model, the KPI definitions, the decision-support logic, the interface, and the traceability between requirements and design. Because the project follows an iterative and incremental method, each design element is assigned to the iteration in which it is implemented: Iteration 1 for scenario setup, what-if simulation, KPI calculation and scenario comparison, and Iteration 2 for decision support and reporting.

   **System Architecture**

   The proposed system is the what-if sandbox of the PuTI digital twin. It does not construct or maintain the actual condition twin. Instead, it uses baseline project and resource data supplied by the companion team and uses it to create, simulate, and compare alternative scenarios.

   Table 4.5 lists the components and their responsibilities.

##### *Table 4.5 System Components* {#table-4.5-system-components}

| Component | Responsibility |
| ----- | ----- |
| Scenario Manager | Creates, configures, saves, and duplicates scenarios based on the eight supported decision situations |
| Simulation Engine | Applies scenario changes to a copy of the baseline and recalculates the schedule and workload using defined simulation rules |
| KPI Calculator and Comparator | Calculates KPIs for the baseline and for each scenario, and computes the difference between them |
| Decision Support Engine | Generates ranked recommendations and the reason for each, based on defined decision criteria |
| Report Generator | Summarises scenario parameters, KPI comparison, and recommended actions |

The technology used to implement the components is Next.js and React for the front-end, PostgreSQL for the database, and Python for the back-end.

   **Use Case Design**

   The users of the system are the people who take part in project-change and resource-allocation decisions in PuTI. The Head of Section and the Assistant Manager approve changes and assign people, and the System Analyst estimates work and screens change requests. The three actors can use all functions, because the decision process in PuTI is shared among them and no role-based restriction was reported in the interviews. Table 4.6 lists the use cases and the requirements they satisfy.

##### *Table 4.6 Use Cases* {#table-4.6-use-cases}

| ID | Use Case | Description |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| UC-01 | Create scenario | The user selects a decision situation (for example, member absence) and creates a scenario from it |
| UC-02 | Configure scenario | The user sets the scenario parameters listed in Table 4.2, and saves or duplicates the scenario |
| UC-03 | Run simulation | The user runs the simulation for a saved scenario |
| UC-04 | View simulation result | The user views the affected project and resource conditions after the simulation |
| UC-05 | View KPIs | The user views the KPIs calculated for the baseline and for the scenario |
| UC-06 | Compare scenarios | The user compares baseline KPIs with one or more scenarios and identifies the best scenario |
| UC-07 | View recommendation | The user views ranked recommended actions and the reason for each |
| UC-08 | Generate report | The user generates a summary of the scenario results and recommended actions |

Each use case is described in more detail as a use case scenario. A use case scenario lists the actor, the precondition, the steps performed by the actor and the responses of the system in the main flow, the alternative flows, and the postcondition. Tables 4.7 to 4.14 present the scenarios for UC-01 to UC-08. The iteration column shows when each use case is implemented, following the two iterations defined in Section III.3.1

   **Simulation Model Design**

   The simulation engine compares a scenario with the baseline. It first takes a copy of the baseline schedule and workload. It then applies the scenario changes to the copy, and recalculates the task schedule and member workload. The calculation follows five steps:

1. Load the baseline snapshot: projects, tasks, dependencies, assignments, member capacity, absences, and holidays.  
2. Apply the scenario changes to the snapshot according to the rule for the selected situation.  
3. Calculate the available capacity of each member for each working day, excluding weekends, holidays, and absences.  
4. Schedule the tasks day by day. A task starts only when its predecessor tasks are finished and an assigned member with the required role has available capacity. The remaining effort of a task is reduced by the capacity allocated to it each day. If a predecessor is delayed, the delay is passed to the dependent task according to the propagation\_factor of the dependency.  
5. Record the simulated start and finish of each task and the load of each member, and pass them to the KPI calculator.  
   Task effort is based on the estimated days in the task record, and the complexity level defines the minimum and maximum days and the load weight of a task. To show the uncertainty of effort, the engine can repeat the run for around 500 replications, in which the effort of each task is drawn between the minimum and maximum days of its complexity level. In this case, the system reports the median and the range of each KPI instead of a single value, so that the results do not appear more precise than they are.

   ![][image9]

   #### [*Figure 4.1. Activity Diagram of the Simulation Process*](https://drive.google.com/file/d/10BT99WS8waJTv4NadeW1ZhL_n4guo-ya/view?usp=sharing) {#figure-4.1.-activity-diagram-of-the-simulation-process}

   Figure 4.1 shows the activity diagram of the simulation process, which is divided into two partitions: the user and the system. The process starts when the user selects the simulation tab, and the system loads the current project snapshot, which is used as the baseline. The user then sets the scenario to run, sets its parameters, and runs it. At this point, the user decides whether to run the scenario only or to run and save it. If the user chooses to run and save, the system first saves the scenario to the database; otherwise, the scenario is run without being stored. In both cases, the system runs the baseline and each scenario using the calculation steps described above. The system then changes each result into KPI values, calculates the difference of each KPI from the baseline, and gives each KPI a status that shows whether it is better or worse than the baseline. Finally, the system displays the result, and the user views the simulation result. 

   **Decision Support Design**

   The decision support function generates recommended actions, such as a replacement resource or extra days, and gives the reason for each. It uses the scenario result and the KPI comparison as input. 

   When a scenario causes overload, delay, or a missed launch target, the system lists candidate actions. For a replacement resource, the candidates are the members whose role matches the affected tasks (or whose secondary role does, if cross-role capable). For extra days, the candidates are extensions of the affected tasks or sprint by a number of working days.

   Each candidate is scored on four criteria taken from the scope: role and skill match, available capacity, the effect on the candidate's current work, and the effect on the KPIs of the scenario. A candidate's score is a weighted sum of these criteria. The candidates are ranked by score.

   For each recommendation the system generates a reason from the criteria values, for example that the member matches the required role, has available capacity of a given number of days in the period, and would reduce the delay by a given number of days while increasing the load of the donor project by a given amount.

   The machine learning component is a supporting component, and it does not make the decision. Because the current data is synthetic, the first version ranks candidates with the transparent scoring above, which can be explained to the stakeholders. A model that learns the ranking from simulated outcomes can be added as part of Iteration 2 if the data supports it. In that case, the model features are role match, skill and seniority, available capacity, current load, and the KPI effect of the action, and its output is a score used in the ranking.

   **Interface Design**

   The interface has five main screens, one for each functional area. Table 4.7 shows the description.

##### *Table 4.15 Interface Screens* {#table-4.15-interface-screens}

| Screen | Main Elements |
| ----- | ----- |
| Scenario setup | List of saved scenarios, selection of decision situation, parameter form based on Table 4.2, save and duplicate buttons |
| Simulation result | Run button, affected projects and tasks, simulated schedule against baseline, member load per period |
| KPI and scenario comparison | KPI table for baseline and selected scenarios, difference and highlight of worse values, best scenario indicator |
| Recommendation | Ranked actions, score, and reason for each |
| Report | Summary of scenario, KPI comparison, and recommended actions, with export |

The user moves through the screens in the order of the process: set up a scenario, run and view the result, compare KPIs. While they can also read the recommendation, and the report will be generated. The user can return to the setup screen from any screen to change the parameters and run the scenario again. Each screen shows the scenario name and the data source (synthetic or PuTI data) so that the user knows which data the results are based on.
